newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Gene foods pose little health risk-Austria study.
newsitem.headline: Gene foods pose little health risk-Austria study.

text.p: Austrian environmentalists were up in arms on Wednesday after a government-funded study showed genetically altered foods posed a negligible risk to consumer health.

"There is no fear that the risk of allergies will increase considerably. The transfer of gene resistance to antibiotics is also very unlikely," scientist Werner Pfannhauser, heading the study, told a news conference.
The findings led to the conclusion that the probability of any risk was so small that it did not justify a complete rejection of gene technology.

Pfannhauser said if a person ate 30 grammes of genetically altered tomatoes every day, it would take up to two years and eight months before the body absorbed one single cell, and even then it was not clear how this would affect the health.
The findings could be embarrassing for the government after it slapped a ban on the import and sale of genetically modified maize last month.
The European Commission two weeks ago said Austria must come up with fresh scientific evidence to warrant a continuation of the ban.
However, sources at the health ministry which imposed the ban said the report would have little impact on its policy.
The study was begun in September 1995 in response to growing concerns of environmental groups and consumers about the potential health hazards of genetically altered foods.
Madeleine Petrovic, Green Party leader, attacked the report for underestimating the possible risks of such foods.
"Just as happened with atomic energy, Austrian scientists have shown they are prepared to play down the dangers of a new technology," she said.
Ulli Sima of pressure group Global 2000 said there were clear parallels with the BSE, or "mad cow", crisis.
"There too scientists for years assured us with studies saying that feeding animals with animal feed was inconceivable," she said.
A handful of Greenpeace activists outside the ministry waved a banner saying "Austrian quality doesn't need gene technology" and offered reporters organically farmed snacks.
A survey accompanying the report showed 61 percent of Austrian consumers did not want gentically engineered foods and nearly 90 percent felt there was not enough information available on the issue.
"One thing the study shows is a lack of research into the safety aspect or testing of genetically engineered foods. Austria urgently needs to fill that gap," Pfannhauser said.

Austria has long been a vocal opponent of genetically modified foods, with two leading supermarket chains refusing to stock them. About half of all organic farms in the European Union are located in Austria.
